title: The soul as a bride
hookLine: many hymns speak as a bride longing for her Husband Lord, a picture of the soul's love

cards: The Gurus were all men. Yet again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, they sing in a woman's voice. A young bride at the window, getting ready, wondering if her beloved will come, asking her friends how they won his love.
Guru Nanak does it. Guru Arjan does it. Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns sit beside theirs, does it too.
Why that voice, of all voices, to speak about God? Today's word opens it: suhagan.

teach.b: Suhagan means the happily married bride, the one united with her husband. Her opposite in the hymns is duhagan, the bride left alone, forgotten.
In this picture, God is the Husband, the Beloved, and every soul is the bride, whether the person singing is a man or a woman. It's not a statement about men and women. It's a picture of love.
In the hymns' picture, the bride can't win love by arguing or bargaining. She can get ready, keep faith, and wait. So how does a bride become suhagan?

Not through jewelry or fancy clothes, the hymns say, but through humility, sweet speech and love. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns in Tilang, the bride is told to go and ask the happy wives how they won the Husband.

The answer, roughly: accept whatever he does as good, drop your own cleverness and your own commands, and do as he says. That's hukam, the order, turned into romance. The picture comes closest to home at a Sikh wedding.
The Laavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung while the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib. They're a wedding song, and also about the soul's marriage to God, stage by stage.

teach.h: THE LAAVAN: TWO WEDDINGS AT ONCE.
teach.b: So every Sikh wedding is two weddings at once.
And the picture says something tender: in these hymns, what lies between a person and God isn't fear or duty. It's longing, and belonging.

how: At a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the four verses of the Laavan by Guru Ram Das are read and sung as the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib, and they're understood as describing both the marriage and the soul's union with God.

s: the bride picture is only about women
every soul is the bride, whether the singer is a man or a woman.
Guru Nanak and Guru Arjan sing in a woman's voice
both sing as the bride, and so does Bhagat Kabir.
in the hymns, the bride wins love through fine jewelry
the hymns say humility, sweet speech and love, not ornaments.

games.q: you're the bride in Guru Nanak's hymn, asking the happy wives how they won his love. what do they tell you?
o: give up your pride, and let him have his way.
games.why: accept what he does as good and drop your own cleverness: humility and surrender to his will, hukam told as a love story.

practice: On paper or in your phone, write one honest line of longing in your own words, for God if that's your language, or for peace, for someone you miss, for the person you hope to become: I wish, I miss, I'm waiting for.
Read it once, quietly. Then set it down and sit with the feeling it leaves, without fixing it.

wordCard.voice: Suhagan. The bride united with her beloved. In the Granth, a picture of the soul, any soul, joined with God through love and humility.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suhagan, the happily married bride; from suhag, the good fortune of a married woman.

carryVoice: Your line: the soul is a bride. The one at the window is still in the love story. That's day two hundred forty-four.
